title: The Author’s Apology for His Book

v: When first I took my pen in hand to write,
I did not know that this would see the light,
or that I’d make a book of such a kind.
I had another book already in mind,
and nearly finished, when, before I knew,
this one had started up, and simply grew.
It happened thus: while writing of the way
the saints must run in this, our gospel day,
I fell into an allegory, a story
about their journey and the road to glory,
in twenty things, or more, which I set down;
and these had hardly settled when I found
another twenty; and they multiplied
like sparks that from a bed of coals fly wide.
Well then, I thought, if you will breed this fast,
I’ll put you by yourselves, lest you at last
go on forever, eating up the book
I was already writing. So I took
you out. But even then I did not think
to show the whole world what my pen and ink
could do in such a style. I only meant
to make, I knew not what, with no intent
to please my neighbor. No, not I: I wrote
to gratify myself. And I would note
that only idle hours went to this,
to turn my mind from thoughts that lead amiss.
So I set pen to paper with delight,
and quickly had my thoughts in black and white;
for once I’d found the thread, it came along
as fast as I could pull; and before long
it grew, for length and breadth, to be the size
of what you now hold open to your eyes.
Well, when I’d put my ends together, I
showed it to others, so that I might try
their judgment: would they condemn or justify?
And some said, Let it live; some, Let it die;
some said, John, print it; others said, Not so;
some said it might do good; and others, No.
Now I was in a strait, and could not see
which was the better thing to do for me.
At last I thought, Since you are so divided,
I’ll print it; and with that the case decided.
For, I thought, some would clearly have it done,
though others in that channel do not run;
so, to find out who had advised the best,
I thought it fit to put it to the test.
And I thought further: should I now deny
the ones who want it, I might, by and by,
be keeping back from them a true delight;
and that, I knew, could never be quite right.
To those who were against its coming out
I said: I’d hate to give offense, no doubt;
yet, since your brothers are so pleased with it,
hold back your judgment till you’ve read a bit.
If you won’t read it, let the thing alone:
some love the meat, and some love picking the bone.
And so that I might soothe them all the more,
I reasoned with them further, as before:
May I not write in such a style as this?
In such a method too, and still not miss
my end, your good? Why should it not be done?
Dark clouds bring water, when the bright bring none.
And dark or bright, if they let fall their drops
of silver, then the earth, by yielding crops,
gives thanks to both, and doesn’t carp at either,
but treasures up the fruit they bring together,
so mingling both that, in the harvest, none
can tell which cloud gave what: the two are one.
They suit her well when hungry; but when full,
she spews out both, and makes their blessings null.
Think of the ways the fisherman will take
to catch his fish; what engines does he make!
See how he brings his whole wit to the task,
his snares, his lines, his hooks, his nets. But ask:
are there not fish that neither hook nor line
nor net nor snare can bring in? Fish so fine
they must be felt for, tickled from their bed,
or they will not be caught, whatever’s said?
And how the fowler works to catch his game
by many means, more than a man could name:
his guns, his nets, his lime-twigs, light, and bell;
he creeps, he walks, he stands; and who can tell
his every posture? Yet not one of these
will make him master of what birds he please.
No, he must pipe and whistle to catch this one,
and, doing that, will find another gone.
If pearls may dwell inside a toad’s head, and
be found in oyster shells along the sand;
if things that promise nothing may contain
what’s worth far more than gold, who will disdain,
once he has had an inkling, there to look,
that he may find it? Now, my little book,
though lacking all the colors that might make
it please this man or that, has, for your sake,
the things in it that far excel the fine
but empty notions where mere fancies shine.
“Well, still, I’m not entirely satisfied
that this your book will stand when soundly tried.”
Why, what’s the matter? “It’s obscure.” So what?
“But it’s made up.” And what of that? Have not
some men, by made-up words as dark as mine,
made truth to sparkle and its rays to shine?
“But they lack solidness.” Speak, man, your mind.
“They drown the weak; metaphors make us blind.”
Solidity, indeed, becomes the pen
of one who writes of things divine to men;
but must I lack solidity because
I speak in metaphors? Were not God’s laws,
his gospel laws, in olden times set forth
by types and shadows, figures? Yet, in truth,
no sober man will dare to find a fault
with those, lest he be found to make assault
on highest wisdom. No, he rather stoops,
and seeks to find out what by pins and loops,
by calves and sheep, by heifers and by rams,
by birds and herbs, and by the blood of lambs,
God speaks to him; and happy is the soul
that finds the light and grace that make them whole.
So don’t be quick to judge, and to conclude
that I lack solidness, that I am crude.
Not all that looks solid is; and we
should not despise a parable, lest we
take in what’s harmful with an easy mind
and lose the good that in it we would find.
My dark and cloudy words, they only hold
the truth, as cabinets enclose the gold.
The prophets often used a metaphor
to set forth truth; and anyone who’s more
than glanced at Christ and his apostles sees
that truth to this day wears such clothes as these.
Am I afraid to say that holy writ,
which for its style and phrase puts down all wit,
is everywhere so full of all these things,
dark figures, allegories? Yet there springs
from that same book the luster, and the rays
of light, that turn our darkest nights to days.
Come, let my critic look at his own life,
where darker lines than any here are rife;
yes, let him look, and he will have to own
that in his best things worse lines can be shown.
Let us but stand before impartial men:
against his one, I’d venture to bet ten
that they will take my meaning in these lines
far better than his, set in silver shrines.
Come, truth, even in swaddling clothes, I find,
informs the judgment, rectifies the mind,
pleases the understanding, makes the will
submit; the memory, too, it serves to fill
with what delights imagination; and
it calms our troubles with a steady hand.
Sound words, I know, Timothy is to use,
and old wives’ fables he is to refuse;
but grave Paul nowhere told him to forbid
the use of parables, in which lay hid
that gold, those pearls, and precious stones that were
worth digging for, and with the greatest care.
Let me add one word more. O man of God,
are you offended? Do you wish I had
put forth my matter in some other way,
or said more plainly what I had to say?
Three things let me propose; then I’ll submit
to those who are my betters, as is fit.
First: nowhere do I find I’m barred from this,
my method, if I use it not amiss,
abusing words or things or readers; nor
am crude in handling figures; but, before
all else, seek to advance the truth. Denied,
did I say? No: I have leave, and at my side
examples, too, from men who pleased God more
by words and ways than any living; wherefore
I may thus speak my mind, and thus declare
things to you that are excellent and rare.
Second: I find that men as tall as trees
write dialogue, and no one slights them. These
are not condemned for writing so. If they
abuse the truth, then cursed be they, I say,
and cursed the craft they use for that intent.
But let the truth be free, in any event,
to make her sallies upon you and me
whichever way God pleases; who but he,
who taught us first to plough, knows how to guide
our minds and pens for his design? And, tried
in his own hand, base things are made to shine
as ushers to the things that are divine.
Third: I find that holy writ in many places
resembles this my method, where the cases
call for one thing to set forth another; so
I may use it too, and yet not overthrow
truth’s golden beams, but by this method may
make them cast forth their rays as bright as day.
And now, before I put away my pen,
I’ll show you what this book is for; and then
commit both you and it into that Hand
that pulls the strong down, and makes weak ones stand.
This book sets out before your very eyes
the man who seeks the everlasting prize;
it shows you where he comes from, where he goes,
what he leaves undone, and also what he does;
it also shows you how he runs, and runs,
until he to the gate of glory comes.
It shows, too, those who set out at full speed,
as if the lasting crown were theirs indeed;
here also you may see the reason why
they lose their labor, and like fools they die.
This book will make a traveler of you,
if you will let its counsel see you through;
it will direct you to the Holy Land,
if its directions you will understand;
yes, it will make the slothful active be,
and make the blind delightful things to see.
Are you for something rare and profitable?
Would you see a truth inside a fable?
Are you forgetful? Would you like to remember
from New Year’s Day to the last of December?
Then read my fancies; they will stick like burs,
and may be, to the helpless, comforters.
This book is written in a dialect
that may the minds of listless men affect:
it seems a novelty, and yet contains
nothing but sound and honest gospel strains.
Would you divert yourself from melancholy?
Would you be pleasant, yet be far from folly?
Would you read riddles, and their explanation?
Or else be drowned in your own contemplation?
Do you love picking at the meat? Or would you
see a man in the clouds, and hear him speak to you?
Would you be in a dream, and yet not sleep?
Or would you, in a moment, laugh and weep?
Would you lose yourself, and catch no harm,
and find yourself again without a charm?
Would you read yourself, and read you know not what,
and yet know whether you are blest or not,
by reading the same lines? Oh, then come hither,
and lay my book, your head, and heart together.
